deep_dive/gs_deep_apple_silicon_001.m4a: Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture is uniquely suited for large models. On a traditional GPU system, model weights sit in VRAM — 24 to 80 gigabytes on consumer hardware. The M3 Ultra provides 512 gigabytes shared between CPU and GPU. No PCIe transfer, no separate pools. The entire memory space is accessible to every compute unit. This is why a desktop Mac can run models that would require a server-class GPU system.
deep_dive/gs_deep_batch_scaling_001.m4a: Batching is free throughput — almost. When you process four requests simultaneously, the model loads weights once but applies them to all four inputs. Memory bandwidth — the main bottleneck for large models — is amortized across the batch. But there are limits. Expert routing in MoE models adds overhead per request. Attention becomes more complex with multiple sequences. And synchronization costs grow. Dense models see about 1.8x speedup per doubling. MoE models, about 1.5x.
deep_dive/gs_deep_context_scaling_001.m4: Why does TPS drop with longer contexts? Three reasons. First, attention is quadratic — the model must attend to every previous token when generating each new one. Second, the KV cache grows linearly, consuming memory bandwidth. Third, as the cache gets larger, hardware cache misses increase. On this cluster, Kimi K2.5 at TP4 drops from 11.5 tokens per second at 1K context to about 1.6 at 8K. That's an 86 percent drop for just 8 times more context.
deep_dive/gs_deep_gqa_001.m4a: Grouped Query Attention is a memory optimization. In standard attention, every query head has its own key and value head. In GQA, groups of query heads share a single key-value pair. Llama 405B has 128 query heads but only 8 key-value heads — a sixteen to one ratio. The queries are diverse, but the keys and values they search against are shared. It's like having 128 detectives searching the same 8 filing cabinets. Surprisingly effective.
deep_dive/gs_deep_kv_cache_001.m4a: The KV cache is the model's memory of the conversation. For every token you've sent and every token the model has generated, it stores key and value vectors at every layer. Llama 405B has 126 layers and 8 key-value heads at 128 dimensions each. That's about 4 kilobytes per token per layer, or roughly half a megabyte per token for the full model. A 32,000-token conversation requires about 16 gigabytes of KV cache alone.
deep_dive/gs_deep_mla_001.m4a: Multi-Latent Attention is an elegant compression trick. Traditional attention stores a full key vector and value vector for every token — thousands of dimensions each. MLA projects these down to just 512 dimensions through a learned bottleneck. When the model needs to attend to past tokens, it reconstructs the full vectors from this compressed representation. The quality loss is minimal, but the memory savings are dramatic — about three to four times less KV cache.
deep_dive/gs_deep_moe_001.m4a: Let me explain how Mixture of Experts works. Imagine a university with hundreds of professors. When a student arrives with a question, a small committee reviews it and assigns it to the most relevant experts. In our models, that committee is a gating network — a tiny neural network that scores each expert's relevance to the current token. Only the top-scoring experts activate. The rest remain dormant, saving compute. Kimi K2.5 has 384 professors. Only 8 teach each student.
deep_dive/gs_deep_quant_001.m4a: Quantization is the art of precision reduction. A model trained in FP16 uses 16 bits per weight — 65,536 possible values. Q4 compresses this to 4 bits — just 16 values per weight. The key insight is that not all precision is created equal. Most weights cluster around a narrow range. By choosing the right scale and offset for each group of weights, we can represent 92 percent of the model's intelligence in one quarter of the memory.
deep_dive/gs_deep_rdma_001.m4a: RDMA — Remote Direct Memory Access — is what makes Tensor Parallel possible on this cluster. Normal networking goes through the kernel: application copies data to kernel, kernel copies to NIC, NIC sends, reverse on the other side. RDMA skips all of that. The GPU writes directly to the remote node's memory through the Thunderbolt 5 interface. No kernel involvement, no copies. That's how we move data between nodes at eighty gigabits per second with microsecond latency.
deep_dive/gs_deep_tp_001.m4a: Tensor Parallel is the most demanding form of distribution. Every matrix multiplication is split — each node computes a slice, then they all exchange results before moving to the next layer. This happens thousands of times per token. The Thunderbolt 5 mesh is critical — at eighty gigabits per second, the communication overhead stays manageable. But the model's dimensions must divide evenly across nodes. That's why TP3 fails for most architectures.

help/gs_help_batch_001.m4a: A personal chef cooks one plate at a time, served the instant it is ready. That is interactive mode. But imagine a banquet — fifty guests arrive at once. A batch kitchen cooks all plates simultaneously, trading individual speed for total throughput. Neither is better. It depends on whether you are feeding one mind or fifty.
help/gs_help_kvcache_001.m4a: The context window is how much the model holds in its head while it thinks. A thousand tokens is about seven hundred words. Four thousand tokens — a few pages of conversation. Thirty-two thousand — an entire document. But every extra page costs memory, and memory costs speed. The art is finding the minimum window that holds your problem.
help/gs_help_model_001.m4a: Think of each model as a different kind of mind. Kimi K2.5 has a trillion parameters — but only the relevant specialists wake for each question, like a hospital that routes you to exactly the right doctor. Llama uses its entire brain on every question — no shortcuts, no routing. The question is not which is better. The question is which matches your problem.
help/gs_help_quant_001.m4a: We cannot fit the entire ocean into a cup, so we fold the water. Q4 folds it four times — the cup is four times smaller, but the water is still ninety-three percent pure. Q2 folds it eight times — fast, light, but the taste changes. FP16 is the unfolded ocean: perfect, enormous, impractical for most cups.
help/gs_help_topology_001.m4a: Imagine a book too large for any single shelf. Tensor Parallel tears out the pages and distributes them across shelves — every shelf works simultaneously. Pipeline Parallel passes the whole book from shelf to shelf — one finishes, hands it to the next. Tensor is faster but requires the Thunderbolt mesh. Pipeline works over Ethernet but adds latency at each hand-off.
help_codex/gs_helpc_benchmarks_001.m4a: The Benchmarks tab shows performance data from real inference runs. Tokens per second across different models, quantization levels, and topology configurations. The numbers come from actual cluster measurements.
help_codex/gs_helpc_hardware_001.m4a: The Hardware tab covers the physical architecture — Apple Silicon chips, Thunderbolt 5 mesh, RDMA fabric, and how the seven nodes connect. Understanding the hardware helps you choose the right topology.
help_codex/gs_helpc_integration_001.m4a: The Integration tab covers deployment and API access. How to set up the TensorZero gateway, connect via OpenAI-compatible API, and monitor the cluster with Prometheus queries.
help_codex/gs_helpc_intelligence_001.m4a: The Intelligence tab explains how different model architectures work — Dense versus Mixture of Experts, Grouped Query Attention versus Multi-Latent Attention. This is the theory behind the numbers.
help_codex/gs_helpc_trials_001.m4a: The Trials tab is where the learning begins. Five tiers of challenges — one for each model family. Complete them to demonstrate your understanding of distributed inference. Each trial teaches a new concept.
help_controls/gs_helpc_claky_001.m4a: The Clacky button! It sends a message to the physical Vestaboard display — a mechanical split-flap board mounted above the monitor. Real atoms flipping for your amusement.
help_controls/gs_helpc_codex_btn_001.m4a: The Codex button opens the knowledge base — hardware reference, benchmarks, architecture guides, and the Resonance Trials. Your learning companion.
help_controls/gs_helpc_deploy_btn_001.m4: The deploy button. Press this to open the deployment wizard and load a model onto the live cluster. Only available in live mode.
help_controls/gs_helpc_fabric_ring_001.m: The fabric health indicator. The coloured ring shows overall cluster health at a glance. Click it to open the detailed cluster view with full telemetry.

help_deploy/gs_helpw_progress_001.m4a: The deployment is in progress. Watch the state machine advance through checking, syncing, configuring, and loading. Each step must complete before the next begins.
help_deploy/gs_helpw_review_001.m4a: Review your deployment. Check the node assignments, verify the model is cached on all target nodes, and confirm the sync requirements. The force sync option re-copies the model even if it already exists.
help_deploy/gs_helpw_topology_001.m4a: First, choose your topology. This decides how many nodes the model will use and how they coordinate. Tensor Parallel is fastest but requires the RDMA mesh. Pipeline works over Ethernet.
help_detail/gs_helpd_deployments_001.m4a: Active deployments shows which models are currently loaded and running on the cluster. Each card shows the model name, topology, and which nodes are involved.
help_detail/gs_helpd_fabric_001.m4a: Fabric efficiency measures how well the distributed topology is performing. Tokens per node shows individual node contribution. The percentage shows efficiency relative to ideal linear scaling.
help_detail/gs_helpd_flow_rate_001.m4a: The flow rate chart tracks tokens per second over time. Look for dips — they indicate contention, thermal throttling, or mesh congestion.
help_detail/gs_helpd_kv_logic_001.m4a: VRAM and KV cache logic shows how the attention cache is managed. KV saturation is the percentage of available cache memory in use. MLA compression shows how much the Multi-Latent Attention mechanism saves.
help_detail/gs_helpd_layer_dist_001.m4a: The layer distribution shows how the model's transformer layers are spread across nodes. In Tensor Parallel, every node processes every layer simultaneously. In Pipeline Parallel, each node handles a subset of layers sequentially.
help_detail/gs_helpd_metrics_preview_001: The metrics preview shows estimated performance for your current configuration. Tokens per second, time to first token, memory per node, power draw, and total RAM usage. These are simulated values — switch to live mode for real measurements.
help_detail/gs_helpd_model_quality_001.m: Model quality shows perplexity — a measure of how confident the model is in its predictions. Lower perplexity means higher quality. The bar goes from CHAOS on the left to GENIUS on the right.
help_detail/gs_helpd_node_memory_001.m4a: Node memory shows how RAM is divided on each node. Cyan is model weights, purple is KV cache, and the remaining space is free. When free memory runs low, performance suffers.
help_detail/gs_helpd_performance_001.m4a: This section shows the cluster's throughput. Tokens per second measures how fast the model generates text. Time to first token shows the startup latency — how long before the first word appears.
help_detail/gs_helpd_stability_001.m4a: The composite stability index combines three factors — base throughput weight, latency floor, and thermal ceiling — into a single score. Higher is better. Below sixty, the cluster is under stress.
help_detail/gs_helpd_telemetry_001.m4a: The telemetry table shows live metrics from every node — throughput, CPU load, GPU temperature, VRAM usage, and network latency. Green rows mean healthy. Red rows mean trouble.
help_detail/gs_helpd_vram_pressure_001.m: VRAM cache pressure shows how full each node's memory is. The bar chart breaks it down per node. When pressure is high, the model may start evicting cached context.
help_mode/gs_helpm_game_001.m4a: Game mode is guided learning. I will walk you through the controls step by step, explain each concept, and challenge you with trials. Start here if you are new to distributed inference.
help_mode/gs_helpm_live_001.m4a: Live mode connects to the real cluster. The numbers are real. The models are running. The Thunderbolt mesh carries actual inference traffic. This is the production environment.
help_mode/gs_helpm_sim_001.m4a: Simulation mode lets you explore freely. Change any parameter and see the estimated effect on performance. No real cluster resources are used — it is a sandbox for experimentation.
help_overview/gs_helpo_cluster_detail_00: Welcome to the detailed cluster view. This panel shows everything happening inside the cluster — throughput charts, per-node telemetry, memory breakdown, stability scores, and fabric efficiency. Take your time exploring each section.
help_overview/gs_helpo_codex_001.m4a: Welcome to the Codex. Five tabs of knowledge — Hardware covers the physical cluster, Benchmarks shows real performance data, Intelligence explains model architectures, Integration covers deployment, and Trials tests your understanding.
help_overview/gs_helpo_sim_panel_001.m4a: This is the simulation panel. From top to bottom — choose your model, set the quantization level, pick a context window, select batch or interactive mode, and choose how to distribute the work across nodes. Each choice affects the metrics below.
help_quick/gs_helpq_batch_001.m4a: Interactive gives fast individual responses. Batch processes many requests at once for higher total throughput.
help_quick/gs_helpq_context_001.m4a: Context length is how many tokens the model remembers during a conversation. More tokens means longer memory, but costs more RAM and slows things down.
help_quick/gs_helpq_model_001.m4a: Choose your model here. Each card shows a different large language model with its architecture and size. Tap a card to simulate how it would perform on the cluster.
help_quick/gs_helpq_quant_001.m4a: Quantization controls how tightly we compress the model. Lower numbers mean smaller but less accurate. Q4 is the sweet spot for most uses.
help_quick/gs_helpq_topology_001.m4a: Topology decides how we spread the model across machines. Single node is simplest. Tensor Parallel splits the work for speed. Pipeline passes it along like a relay.
hover_tip/gs_hover_batch_001.m4a: Batch size — how many requests the model processes simultaneously. Batch one means dedicated attention. Higher batches increase total throughput but add latency per request.
hover_tip/gs_hover_context_001.m4a: Context window — how many tokens the model can see at once. One token is roughly three quarters of a word. A 32K window holds about 24,000 words. A 256K window could hold an entire novel.
hover_tip/gs_hover_ep_001.m4a: Embarrassingly Parallel — each node runs a complete copy of the model independently. No coordination needed. Perfect for serving multiple users, but each node needs enough memory for the full model.
hover_tip/gs_hover_flow_rate_001.m4a: Flow rate — a real-time chart of tokens per second over the last sixty seconds. Dips indicate context scaling, KV cache pressure, or RDMA synchronization pauses.
hover_tip/gs_hover_gqa_001.m4a: Grouped Query Attention. Multiple query heads share a single key-value head. Llama 405B uses a 16-to-1 ratio — 128 query heads but only 8 key-value heads. This reduces KV cache without losing much quality.
hover_tip/gs_hover_kv_cache_001.m4a: The KV cache stores attention state for every token in the conversation. It grows with context length. GQA models need about four kilobytes per token per layer. MLA models compress this to about one kilobyte.
hover_tip/gs_hover_mesh_001.m4a: The mesh visualization shows the five compute nodes and their Thunderbolt 5 connections. Green links are healthy. Animated particles show data flowing between nodes during inference.
hover_tip/gs_hover_mla_001.m4a: Multi-Latent Attention. Instead of storing full key and value vectors, MLA compresses them through a low-rank bottleneck. The rank is 512 dimensions, compared to thousands in traditional attention. This cuts KV cache by a factor of three to four.
hover_tip/gs_hover_model_card_001.m4a: The model card shows architecture details — parameter count, layer depth, attention type, context window, and which topologies are compatible. Not all models fit all configurations.
hover_tip/gs_hover_moe_001.m4a: Mixture of Experts. The model has many expert networks but only activates a few per token. A small gating network decides which experts to use. This lets the model be large without the cost of being large.
hover_tip/gs_hover_node_temp_001.m4a: Node temperature. The M3 Ultra throttles at about 108 degrees Celsius. Distributed inference spreads the heat — four nodes at 70 degrees each is safer than one node at 95.
hover_tip/gs_hover_perplexity_001.m4a: Perplexity measures prediction confidence. Lower is better. FP16 is the reference at one hundred percent quality. Each quantization level trades a bit of quality for major memory savings.
hover_tip/gs_hover_pp_001.m4a: Pipeline Parallel chains nodes in sequence. Each node processes a subset of layers. Simpler than Tensor Parallel, but adds latency proportional to the number of stages.
hover_tip/gs_hover_quant_001.m4a: Quantization compresses model weights. Lower bits means smaller size and faster speed, but reduced quality. Q4 is the sweet spot — about seven percent quality loss for a quarter of the memory.
hover_tip/gs_hover_stability_001.m4a: Composite Stability Index. A score from zero to one hundred measuring overall cluster health — temperature, memory pressure, RDMA fabric status, and inference consistency. Above ninety is healthy.
hover_tip/gs_hover_topology_001.m4a: Topology is how we arrange the nodes for computation. Single node is simplest. Tensor Parallel for large models that need more memory. Pipeline for depth. Embarrassingly Parallel for throughput.
hover_tip/gs_hover_tp_001.m4a: Tensor Parallel splits each layer across multiple nodes. Every node processes a piece of every token simultaneously. This requires fast interconnect — our Thunderbolt 5 mesh runs at eighty gigabits per second.
hover_tip/gs_hover_tps_001.m4a: Tokens per second. How fast the model generates output. Higher is better for interactive chat. Lower is expected for larger models or longer contexts.
hover_tip/gs_hover_ttft_001.m4a: Time to first token. The delay before the model starts responding. This includes reading your entire prompt. Longer prompts mean longer waits.
hover_tip/gs_hover_vram_001.m4a: VRAM — the memory inside each node's GPU. Models, KV cache, and operating system all compete for this space. At 512 gigabytes per node, we have room, but large models fill it fast.

idle_factoid/gs_factoid_001.m4a: Did you know? Llama 405B has 126 layers. That's deeper than most buildings are tall. Each layer transforms every token, adding understanding.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_002.m4a: The Mixtral paper proved that MoE could work at production scale. Before December 2023, most MoE models were research curiosities. After Mixtral, everyone built one.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_003.m4a: Multi-Latent Attention was introduced by DeepSeek in their V2 paper. Instead of storing full K and V vectors, it projects them through a 512-dimensional bottleneck. The compression ratio is remarkable.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_004.m4a: Grouped Query Attention was first popularized by Llama 2. The insight is simple — multiple query heads can share key-value pairs without losing much quality. Llama 405B uses a 16-to-1 ratio.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_005.m4a: The M3 Ultra in each compute node has 512 gigabytes of unified memory. CPU and GPU share it all. No PCIe bottleneck, no separate VRAM. That's the Apple Silicon advantage.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_006.m4a: Thunderbolt 5 runs at 80 gigabits per second with peaks up to 120 using bandwidth boost. That's fast enough to transfer a 4-bit Qwen 32B model in under two seconds.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_007.m4a: Why can't most models do TP3? Because their hidden dimensions are powers of two — 4096, 5120, 7168, 16384. None of these divide evenly by three.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_008.m4a: Kimi K2.5 has 384 experts — more than any other model in our collection. But only 8 activate per token. That's a 2 percent activation rate. Extreme sparsity, extreme efficiency.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_009.m4a: Q4 quantization stores each weight in 4 bits. That's 16 possible values per weight. The magic is in how we choose those 16 values — the right scale and zero-point can preserve most of the model's intelligence.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_010.m4a: DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2.5 share the same attention innovation — MLA. Both have a KV low-rank of 512. But Kimi has 384 experts compared to DeepSeek's 256. More experts, finer specialization.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_011.m4a: The attention mechanism has quadratic complexity with sequence length. Double the context, quadruple the attention computation. That's why long contexts are expensive.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_012.m4a: Qwen 2.5 uses YaRN for extended context. The base model was trained at 32,000 tokens but YaRN — Yet Another RoPE Extension — stretches it to 131,000. Math tricks that let the model see farther.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_013.m4a: MoE experts do not specialize by subject — a common misconception. They specialize by syntax and structure patterns. One expert might handle noun phrases while another handles conditional logic.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_014.m4a: Metal's sixty-second GPU timeout is a hardware safety feature. Apple designed it to prevent runaway compute from crashing the system. Unfortunately, it also limits how long a prefill can take.
idle_factoid/gs_factoid_015.m4a: RDMA — Remote Direct Memory Access — bypasses the operating system entirely. Data moves directly between GPUs across nodes. No TCP overhead, no kernel copies. That's how we hit eighty gigabits.

model_chatter_deepseek/gs_chatter_deepse: DeepSeek uses Multi-Latent Attention, just like Kimi. It compresses the key-value cache dramatically. Long contexts become practical even at this scale.
Six hundred and seventy-one billion parameters, but only thirty-seven billion active per token. The routing efficiency is remarkable — less than six percent of the network fires for each question.
DeepSeek excels at mathematics and code. The architecture was designed for precise, structured reasoning. It thinks in patterns, not guesses.
One hundred and thirty-one thousand tokens of context, with the MLA compression keeping memory manageable. You can feed it enormous codebases without drowning in KV cache.
At TP4, DeepSeek runs at twenty-six tokens per second. Fast for a model of this size. The MoE architecture pays for itself in throughput.

DeepSeek V3 was trained for about 5.5 million dollars — a fraction of what comparable models cost. The MoE architecture means less compute per training step, even though the total parameter count is massive.
61 layers, 128 attention heads, and a hidden dimension of 7168. DeepSeek and Kimi share these exact same dimensions. The difference is in expert count — DeepSeek has 256, Kimi scales to 384.

DeepSeek V3 uses auxiliary-loss-free load balancing. Traditional MoE adds an extra loss term to prevent expert collapse — where all tokens route to the same expert. DeepSeek found a way to balance without it.
MLA compresses the KV cache from about 4 kilobytes per token per layer down to about 1.15 kilobytes. Over 61 layers and thousands of tokens, that compression saves hundreds of gigabytes.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_001.m: One trillion parameters. And yet only thirty-two billion activate for each question. The rest wait in silence, ready if called. Efficiency is not laziness — it is wisdom.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_002.m: Kimi uses Multi-Latent Attention. Instead of storing full key-value pairs, it compresses them. The memory savings are enormous — this is how we fit a trillion parameters across just four nodes.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_003.m: This model has a massive context window — two hundred and fifty-six thousand tokens. You could feed it an entire codebase and it would hold the whole thing in its mind at once.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_004.m: Notice the routing. Each token is examined by a tiny gating network that decides which experts to wake. The decision happens in microseconds. A trillion neurons, but only the relevant thirty-two billion fire.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_005.m: At Q4, Kimi needs about six hundred gigabytes of memory. That is why we need the full cluster — four nodes in Tensor Parallel, sharing the load across the Thunderbolt mesh.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_006.m: Kimi K2.5 and DeepSeek V3 share the same attention design — Multi-Latent Attention with a KV low-rank of 512. But Kimi takes the expert count from 256 to 384. More options for the gating network to choose from.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_007.m: At TP4, Kimi generates 11.5 tokens per second. At TP2, just 4 tokens per second. The difference? Memory bandwidth. At TP4, each node holds 153 gigabytes — loads in seconds. At TP2, 306 gigabytes — near the Metal timeout.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_008.m: Kimi K2.5 has 61 layers. The same depth as DeepSeek V3. They're architectural siblings — same MLA, same layer count, different expert scaling. Kimi traded depth for breadth.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_009.m: A 256K context window means Kimi can hold about 192,000 words in its mind at once. That's three full novels. Or an entire large codebase with documentation.
model_chatter_kimi/gs_chatter_kimi_010.m: Kimi's hidden dimension is 7168. This divides by 2 and 4 but not by 3 or 5. That's why TP2 and TP4 work, but TP3 and TP5 fail with a shard error.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_001: Four hundred and five billion parameters, all active, all the time. No shortcuts. This is brute force intelligence.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_002: Llama 405B does not fit on a single node. Even at Q4, it needs two hundred and twenty gigabytes. That is why Tensor Parallel exists — we split the mind across the mesh.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_003: One hundred and twenty-six layers deep. One hundred and twenty-eight attention heads. This is the architecture that taught the world that scale still matters.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_004: Every token in Llama passes through all four hundred and five billion parameters. No gating, no routing. The entire network thinks about every word you say. That is expensive, but thorough.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_005: At TP4, Llama runs at about twenty-two tokens per second on this cluster. Not the fastest, but the depth of understanding is unmatched for a dense model.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_006: Llama 405B has 128 attention heads but only 8 key-value heads. That's a sixteen-to-one GQA ratio — the most aggressive KV compression of any dense model in our collection. Sixteen queries searching the same eight filing cabinets.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_007: With a hidden dimension of 16384, Llama has the widest layers in our collection. Each attention head operates on 128 dimensions. Wide layers mean rich representations — the model can encode more nuance per position.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_008: Llama 3.1 was released by Meta in July 2024. The 405B variant was the first truly open model to compete with the best proprietary systems. It proved that scale plus open access changes everything.
model_chatter_llama/gs_chatter_llama_009: 126 layers deep. That means each token passes through 126 sequential transformations before the model produces an output. In Pipeline Parallel, we split these layers across nodes — 63 layers each in PP2, 32 each in PP4.
model_chatter_mixtral/gs_chatter_mixtral: Eight groups of experts, seven billion parameters each. But for any given token, only two groups activate. The rest wait patiently.
Mixtral is the fastest model in our collection. Nearly a hundred tokens per second on a single node. Speed and efficiency in perfect balance.
The context window is thirty-two thousand tokens — shorter than the others, but still enough for a complete document or a long conversation.
This was the model that proved Mixture of Experts could work in practice. Before Mixtral, MoE was theoretical. After Mixtral, everyone built one.
At Q4, Mixtral needs only twenty-six gigabytes. It fits easily on a single node with memory to spare. Perfect for quick iteration.

Mixtral routes each token to exactly two of eight experts. The gating network produces a probability distribution over all experts and selects the top two. The expert outputs are combined with learned weights.

46.7 billion total parameters, but only 12.9 billion activate per token. That means you pay for 46.7 billion in memory but only 12.9 billion in compute. Storage cost is the price of expertise diversity.
Mixtral's context window is 32,000 tokens — the shortest in our collection. But 32K is still about 24,000 words. For most conversations and code tasks, that's more than enough.
Mixtral was released by Mistral AI in December 2023. A French company proved that a small team with the right architecture could compete with labs ten times their size.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_001.m: Qwen 32B is a dense model. Every single parameter fires on every question. No routing, no wasted experts. What you see is what you get.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_002.m: At Q4, Qwen fits comfortably on a single node — just eighteen gigabytes. Fast, efficient, and reliable. The workhorse of the cluster.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_003.m: Qwen supports one hundred and thirty-one thousand tokens of context. For a thirty-two billion parameter model, that is remarkably generous. You could feed it an entire project.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_004.m: Grouped Query Attention. Qwen shares key-value heads across multiple query heads. This reduces memory without sacrificing quality. A clever architectural choice.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_005.m: This is the model I recommend for beginners. Small enough to run on a single machine, smart enough to hold its own against models ten times its size.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_006.m: Qwen 2.5 uses forty attention heads with eight key-value heads — a five-to-one GQA ratio. Five queries share each key-value pair. Efficient, but not as compressed as Llama's sixteen-to-one.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_007.m: The base Qwen 32B was trained on 32,000 tokens of context. YaRN extends it to 131,000. The trick is modifying the rotary position embeddings — the mathematical encoding that tells the model where each token sits.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_008.m: Qwen's hidden dimension is 5120. That divides evenly by 1, 2, 4, and 5 — so TP5 actually works for this model. But at 32 billion parameters, why would you distribute it? It runs perfectly on one node.
model_chatter_qwen/gs_chatter_qwen_009.m: 32.5 billion parameters. Not a round number, but that's what 64 layers of 5120-dimensional transformations with 40-head attention adds up to. Every parameter earned its place.
model_commentary/gs_model_deepseek_001.m: DeepSeek V3. Six hundred and seventy-one billion parameters, but only thirty-seven billion wakes for each question. Mathematical elegance — sparse routing at enormous scale.
model_commentary/gs_model_deepseek_002.m: DeepSeek V3. A six hundred and seventy-one billion parameter mind with the efficiency of a much smaller one. The routing is what makes it special.
model_commentary/gs_model_deepseek_003.m: DeepSeek V3 has 256 experts with a top-8 routing strategy. But here's the clever part — it also has shared experts that always activate. A mix of specialized and general knowledge.
model_commentary/gs_model_kimi_k25_001.m: Kimi K2.5. A one trillion parameter mind, but only thirty-two billion wakes for each question — like a hospital of specialists. You do not summon every doctor for a headache.
model_commentary/gs_model_kimi_k25_002.m: Kimi K2.5. One trillion parameters. The largest mind in our collection. But it is efficient — only the relevant experts activate. A trillion neurons, thirty-two billion voices.
model_commentary/gs_model_kimi_k25_003.m: Kimi K2.5. Sixty-one layers, sixty-four attention heads, and 384 routed experts. The architecture is a scaled descendant of DeepSeek V3 — same MLA attention, but with fifty percent more experts.
Llama 405B. Four hundred and five billion parameters, every one active on every question. No routing, no shortcuts. It needs the memory to match its ambition.
Llama 405B. The leviathan. Four hundred and five billion parameters — dense, powerful, uncompromising. It demands the full cluster.
Llama 405B. One hundred and twenty-six layers and one hundred and twenty-eight attention heads. Meta's philosophy is simple — make it bigger, make it denser, and scale will do the rest.
model_commentary/gs_model_mixtral_001.m4: Mixtral 8x7B. Eight groups of seven billion experts. Only two groups activate per question. Fast, efficient, and surprisingly capable for its size.
model_commentary/gs_model_mixtral_002.m4: Mixtral 8x7B. A clever design — eight experts, but you only pay for two at a time. The rest sleep until they are needed.
model_commentary/gs_model_mixtral_003.m4: Mixtral uses Grouped Query Attention with a four-to-one ratio — thirty-two query heads sharing eight key-value heads. Combined with MoE, it's doubly efficient.
model_commentary/gs_model_qwen32b_001.m4: Qwen 32B. A dense model — all thirty-two billion parameters active on every question. Fast, smart, fits on a single machine. A great first choice.
model_commentary/gs_model_qwen32b_002.m4: Qwen 32B. Thirty-two billion parameters, every single one awake for you. No routing, no wasted capacity. Clean and focused.
model_commentary/gs_model_qwen32b_003.m4: Qwen 2.5 is Apache-licensed. Open weights, open code. You can study every layer, modify every head. Knowledge should be free.

quant_commentary/gs_quant_fp16_003.m4a: Full precision. Sixteen bits per weight. The model exactly as the researchers trained it. Maximum fidelity, maximum memory. Reserve this for when quality is everything.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q2_001.m4a: Q2. We have crushed the library into a single, dusty shelf. The thoughts will fly fast, but do not trust the shadows they cast.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q2_002.m4a: Q2. Two bits per weight. The model will hallucinate. It will be fast, it will be small, but the answers may be fiction. Proceed with caution.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q2_003.m4a: Q2. The most aggressive compression. The model loses significant intelligence. Only useful for speed testing, not for truth.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q3_001.m4a: Q3. We are folding hard now. The water is getting cloudy — like photocopying a photocopy.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q3_002.m4a: Q3. Three bits per weight. The model gets noticeably worse at reasoning and nuance. Use this only when memory is truly scarce.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q3_003.m4a: Q3. Three bits per weight. We're crossing into lossy territory now. The model will sound confident but may stumble on nuance. Watch the perplexity indicator.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q4_001.m4a: Q4. The sweet spot, and I do not say that lightly. Four times smaller, ninety-three percent of the truth. Most people stop here for good reason.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q4_002.m4a: Q4. Four bits per weight. The model is four times smaller than full precision but retains ninety-three percent of the original quality. This is where most practitioners land.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q4_003.m4a: Q4. I recommend this for almost everyone. The compression is aggressive but the intelligence survives. The sweet spot between speed and truth.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q4_004.m4a: Q4. Four bits per weight. A quarter the size of FP16. On Apple Silicon, the quantized kernels actually run faster than full precision — memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, not compute.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q6_001.m4a: Q6. A smart fold. Still clear, and the cup is noticeably lighter.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q6_002.m4a: Q6. Six bits per weight. You save forty percent of the memory and the quality barely shifts. Good for when Q8 is just a little too heavy.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q6_003.m4a: Q6. Six bits per weight. Almost imperceptible quality loss — about three percent. A gentle squeeze that saves significant memory.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q8_001.m4a: Q8. We fold the water gently. Nearly lossless — you would struggle to taste what changed.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q8_002.m4a: Q8. Eight-bit quantization. Half the memory of full precision, and the quality loss is practically invisible. A wise balance.
quant_commentary/gs_quant_q8_003.m4a: Q8. Eight bits per weight — half the memory of FP16, and the quality loss is practically invisible. If you have the space, this is the best compression.

quant_mood_fp16/gs_quant_mood_fp16_003.m: Full precision. Every weight at its true value. But the memory cost is enormous.
quant_mood_fp16/gs_quant_mood_fp16_004.m: F P 16 — maximum fidelity. The question is whether you have the memory for it.

quant_mood_q2/gs_quant_mood_q2_004.m4a: Two bits per weight. It's like photocopying a photocopy of a photocopy. Fast though.

topo_commentary/gs_topo_tp2_003.m4a: Two nodes in Tensor Parallel. Each one holds half the model. They split every matrix multiply and sync over Thunderbolt at eighty gigabits per second.

topo_mood_pp/gs_topo_mood_pp_002.m4a: Pipeline mode. The work flows like water through pipes — sequential, predictable, but each joint adds a moment of delay.
topo_mood_pp/gs_topo_mood_pp_003.m4a: Pipeline parallel. Each stage processes its layers, then passes the baton.
topo_mood_pp/gs_topo_mood_pp_004.m4a: Sequential processing. Watch the time to first token — pipelines add latency.
topo_mood_single/gs_topo_mood_single_001: One node. One mind. Simple and clean. No synchronisation needed — just thought.
topo_mood_single/gs_topo_mood_single_002: Solo performance. One node, full attention, zero communication overhead. Sometimes simplicity wins.
topo_mood_single/gs_topo_mood_single_003: One node doing all the work. Simple and clean. No network overhead.
topo_mood_single/gs_topo_mood_single_004: Solo mode. If the model fits, this is always the fastest option.
topo_mood_tp2/gs_topo_mood_tp2_002.m4a: Two nodes sharing the load. Halves the memory, keeps things fast.
topo_mood_tp2/gs_topo_mood_tp2_003.m4a: Tensor parallel across two. Clean split — each node handles half the attention heads.
topo_mood_tp2/gs_topo_mood_tp2_004.m4a: T P 2 is a good balance. Not too complex, big memory saving.
topo_mood_tp4/gs_topo_mood_tp4_001.m4a: Four nodes in Tensor Parallel! The full formation. The Thunderbolt mesh carries their thoughts at eighty gigabits per second. A symphony of silicon.
topo_mood_tp4/gs_topo_mood_tp4_002.m4a: The cluster breathes as one. Four minds, four hundred gigabytes of unified memory. This is distributed intelligence at its finest.
topo_mood_tp4/gs_topo_mood_tp4_003.m4a: TP4. The silicon choir. Four nodes breathing as one, synchronized down to the microsecond across the RDMA mesh.
topo_mood_tp4/gs_topo_mood_tp4_004.m4a: Four nodes in a full mesh. The Thunderbolt fabric is working hard on this one.
topo_mood_tp4/gs_topo_mood_tp4_005.m4a: T P 4 — the go-to for big models. Quarter the memory per node.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep2_001.m4a: Two independent copies. Each node serves its own requests — double the throughput, zero coordination overhead.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep2_002.m4a: Embarrassingly Parallel with two nodes. Two scholars, two desks, two separate books. They never need to speak to each other.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep2_003.m4a: Two-way replication. The model runs twice, independently. If one user asks a question, the other node is free for someone else.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep3_001.m4a: Three independent copies. Three scholars, three separate desks. Triple the throughput without a single message between them.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep3_002.m4a: Embarrassingly Parallel across three nodes. No synchronisation, no waiting. Each node is its own island of inference.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep3_003.m4a: Three-way replication. Three minds, each working alone. The simplest way to serve three users simultaneously.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep4_001.m4a: Four independent copies running in parallel. Four scholars, four separate books. Maximum throughput for concurrent users.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep4_002.m4a: Embarrassingly Parallel with four nodes. No coordination overhead whatsoever. Each node is sovereign.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep4_003.m4a: Four-way replication. The model runs four times, each instance fully independent. Pure horizontal scaling.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep5_001.m4a: Five scholars, five different books. Each reads independently — maximum variety, zero coordination.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep5_002.m4a: The entire cluster running independently. Five nodes, five copies, five users served simultaneously. The ultimate throughput configuration.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_ep5_003.m4a: All five scholars, each with their own complete book. No coordination needed. The simplest distributed strategy — and sometimes the wisest.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp2_001.m4a: Pipeline across two machines. A bucket brigade — each scholar reads one chapter, then passes the bucket forward. More hands means more memory, but each hand-off costs time.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp2_002.m4a: Two-stage pipeline. Node one processes the first half of the layers, node two finishes. Sequential, but it lets us fit larger models.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp2_003.m4a: Pipeline Parallel across two nodes. The first scholar reads the early chapters, passes the result forward. Doubles the memory, but adds a hand-off delay.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp3_001.m4a: Pipeline across three machines. Three links in the chain, three scholars passing the bucket. More memory — but three hand-offs to wait for.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp3_002.m4a: Three-stage pipeline. The model splits into thirds. Each node handles its layers in sequence. The price of memory is latency.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp3_003.m4a: A three-node bucket brigade. Each scholar reads their chapter and passes the result forward. Fits larger models at the cost of response time.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp4_001.m4a: Pipeline across four machines. A longer bucket brigade. Much more memory, but the latency grows with every link in the chain.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp4_002.m4a: Four-stage pipeline. Four nodes, each bearing a quarter of the layers. Enough memory for the largest models — but four sequential hand-offs.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp4_003.m4a: Pipeline across four machines. A longer chain means more memory, but each link adds latency. Use this when the model simply will not fit any other way.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp5_001.m4a: Pipeline across all five machines. The longest chain. Maximum memory — but five hand-offs of latency. Only for the truly enormous models.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp5_002.m4a: Five stages of pipeline. Each node holds one-fifth of the layers. The memory is vast, but the latency grows with every link.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_pp5_003.m4a: The full five-node pipeline. A bucket brigade stretching across the entire cluster. Patience is the price of holding the largest minds.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_single_001.m: One scholar, one book. No coordination needed. Sometimes the simplest path is the wisest.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_single_002.m: A single mind, undivided. No messages to pass, no synchronisation to manage. The fastest path — when the model fits.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_single_003.m: Single node inference. No synchronization, no network overhead. If the model fits, this is always the fastest option.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp2_001.m4a: Tensor Parallel across two machines. The scholars tear out the pages and read their fragments aloud in perfect synchronisation. Fastest response — but they must stay in lockstep.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp2_002.m4a: Two nodes in Tensor Parallel. Every matrix split in half, computed simultaneously. The Thunderbolt mesh carries the synchronisation at eighty gigabits per second.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp2_003.m4a: Two nodes in Tensor Parallel. Each one holds half the model. They split every matrix multiply and sync over Thunderbolt at eighty gigabits per second.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp3_001.m4a: Tensor Parallel across three machines. Three nodes splitting every computation. But be warned — not every model divides cleanly by three.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp3_002.m4a: Three-way Tensor Parallel. The attention heads must divide evenly by three. If they do, the speed is remarkable. If not — the model will refuse.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp3_003.m4a: TP3. Three scholars reading in lockstep, each taking a third of every matrix. Powerful — when the architecture permits it.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp4_001.m4a: Tensor Parallel across four machines. Four scholars reading in lockstep. The fastest formation — the Thunderbolt mesh carries their whispers at the speed of light.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp4_002.m4a: TP4. The sweet spot for our cluster. Four scholars reading in perfect lockstep — every matrix divided into quarters, every result gathered at the speed of light.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp4_003.m4a: Tensor Parallel across four machines. Four nodes, computing every layer together. The Thunderbolt mesh sings with synchronisation.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp5_001.m4a: Tensor Parallel across all five nodes. The entire cluster working as one mind. But five-way splits are demanding — the architecture must cooperate.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp5_002.m4a: Five-way Tensor Parallel. Every attention head, every matrix, split five ways. The coordination is extraordinary — but so are the constraints.
topology_commentary/gs_topo_tp5_003.m4a: TP5. The full cluster in lockstep. Maximum parallelism — but most models cannot divide their dimensions by five. Check the architecture first.
